title: A Brief History of Air Travel
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry in the booth) trace the history of passenger air travel in a loosely chronological way: the 1914 St. Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line flight, early airmail under the US Postal Service, the 1920s rich-only era, early plane cabins and noise, the origins of airline terminology borrowed from steamships, the rise of stewardesses and nurse flight attendants (Ellen Church), early women pilots, airplane bathrooms and vacuum toilets, the Boeing 247 and Douglas DC-3, 1930s-1950s dining and smoking, airport desegregation, the jet age (Boeing 707, 747), the 1978 airline deregulation under Jimmy Carter, discount airlines, in-flight entertainment and Wi-Fi, defunct airlines, and a listener mail letter about a cat named Toots.

segments.title: Opening banter on Wings and the episode premise
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the TV show Wings and introduce the episode as a walk through the timeline of passenger air travel, excluding plane mechanics, crashes and hijackings.

segments.title: First passenger flights and early airmail
segments.summary: The 1914 St. Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line flight is described, along with its fares and short run. Early international flights from Florida to Cuba by Aeromarine Airways are mentioned. The US government's airmail flights beginning in 1918 are covered, including the inverted Jenny stamp, and mail was later handed to private companies.

segments.title: 1920s-1930s early passenger planes and noise
segments.summary: Early passenger flying in the 1920s was expensive and exclusive, with about 6,000 passengers in 1929. Early planes were cold, loud, unpressurized and bumpy, such as the Ford Tri-Motor, and LaGuardia had a skywalk where people watched takeoffs.

segments.title: Steamship terminology in aviation
segments.summary: Early airline terms such as steward, captain and airline were borrowed from ships, partly because many early planes were airboats that operated on water.

segments.title: Stewards to stewardesses and Ellen Church
segments.summary: Early flight attendants were male stewards. Nurse Ellen Church, who worked for Boeing, hired the first eight stewardesses, all nurses. The term flight attendant replaced stewardess in the late 1970s, slowly.

segments.title: Early women pilots
segments.summary: Women became commercial pilots starting in 1969 with Terry Whideroo at Scandinavian Air Systems, followed by Emily Howell Warner at Frontier and Bonnie Tobersky at American in 1973. Warner became the first female captain around 1976. The hosts discuss the age of a 24-year-old pilot.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with an ad read.

segments.title: Boeing 247, Douglas DC-3 and 1930s aircraft
segments.summary: The Boeing 247 of 1933 offered an insulated cabin, cushioned seats, hot and cold water and food service. The Douglas DC-3, with 21 seats and a galley, came to dominate, making up about ninety percent of planes by the end of the 1930s. A DC-3 flown in Finland in 2021 is mentioned.

segments.title: Airplane bathrooms and vacuum toilets
segments.summary: Early plane toilets were essentially buckets or holding tanks. James Kemper invented the vacuum-flush airplane toilet, which uses suction rather than releasing waste into the air. A 747 flight produces about 230 gallons of sewage. Frozen blue ice from lavatory leaks can fall and injure people, though it is rarely a body-matter myth as shown in Six Feet Under.

segments.title: 1930s-1950s airline dining and service
segments.summary: Early airline meals were elaborate, with carved meats and multi-course service, with the ticket including this treatment. Limited planes made it easier to prepare fancy meals. Airlines competed by treating passengers like royalty, such as United's red carpet on its DC-7.

segments.title: Airport segregation in the South
segments.summary: Airlines were not segregated, but many airports were. Washington National Airport ended segregation in 1948 after NAACP protests. The DOJ sued Southern airports in the 1960s. Shreveport, Louisiana had the last airport desegregated, in 1963.

segments.title: The jet age, Boeing 707 and 747
segments.summary: Jet travel became widespread around 1958. Igor Cassini coined the term jet set in the early 1950s. The Boeing 707 cut transatlantic flight time roughly in half and carried more passengers. The Boeing 747 was called the Queen of the Skies and had lounges and bars.

segments.title: Airplane lounges, ticket prices and 1960s-70s advertising
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the lost plane lounges and bars, including Virgin's bars and Concorde-like experiences, and cost comparisons: a 1970 New York to London round trip was about five thousand dollars, versus about 586 dollars today on British Airways. Airline advertising in the 1960s and 70s used flirtatious stewardesses to attract business travelers.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with an ad read.

segments.title: Smoking on airplanes
segments.summary: Airlines handed out cigarettes and encouraged smoking through the 1970s, which harmed flight attendants. A 1997 settlement of about 300 million dollars from the tobacco industry followed. Smoking sections came in 1971, California banned smoking within the state in 1987, a federal rule came in 1990, and Delta became the first airline to ban smoking in 1995. Ashtrays remain on planes by federal law.

segments.title: In-flight food evolution and Pan Am
segments.summary: Early meals were served during refueling stops in hangars. Pan American Airways developed airline meals that predated TV dinners, which came along in the 1950s.

segments.title: 1978 airline deregulation and discount airlines
segments.summary: President Jimmy Carter signed the 1978 bill deregulating the US airline industry. Airlines cut frills and competition increased, but over time consolidation followed. Pacific Southwest Airlines was the first discount airline, starting cut-rate seats in 1949, and Laker Airways was another budget carrier. Delta ran ads opposing deregulation.

segments.title: In-flight entertainment history
segments.summary: Air Marine Airways showed a promotional film, Howdy Chicago, in 1921. TWA first offered in-flight movies in 1961, and overhead screens followed in the 1960s. Pneumatic-tube headsets were used until Delta phased them out in 2003. Seatback screens came with Northwest Airlines in 1988, and Wi-Fi arrived in 2003 with British Airways and Lufthansa.

segments.title: Defunct and memorable airlines
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Hooters Air, flight attendant outfits, Mohawk Airline (with the first African American flight attendant), ValuJet, Eastern Airlines, AirTran's loyalty program, and Midwest Airlines, which baked cookies on board and had all one class. They discuss rising fares since COVID and greedflation.

segments.title: Listener mail from Lou about his cat Toots
segments.summary: Listener Lou writes that his childhood cat Toots died and that the hosts' episodes on dumb criminals and death helped him cope. The hosts send condolences and invite listener email.

segments.summary: Closing credits and iHeartRadio promotion.
